item.title: Navigating the Cyclospora Outbreak
item.description:
Health

Navigating the Cyclospora Outbreak

How to stay safe from Cyclospora risk without compromising nutrition.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Cyclospora is a parasite that is generally transmitted when infected feces contaminate food or water.
  • The name of the illness caused by the Cyclospora parasite is cyclosporiasis.
  • Canned or frozen produce generally carries a lower risk than fresh produce.
Source: Marzena7 / Pixabay

Recent headlines and social media feeds have become dominated by the news of the Cyclospora outbreak. Like many people, you may have seen an ongoing stream of posts, videos, and updates covering the situation. With so much information available, it can easily become overwhelming to try and keep up with the latest updates and developments.

Although the word Cyclospora has been discussed a lot in the media, some people don’t really know what it means. According to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Cyclospora is a parasite that is generally transmitted when infected feces contaminate food or water.¹ Due to this, it is highly unlikely for Cyclospora to be transmitted from one person to another. Unlike many other foodborne illnesses, people typically become infected after consuming contaminated food rather than through direct contact with someone who is sick. This is one reason why identifying the exact source of an outbreak can be so challenging.

The name of the illness caused by the Cyclospora parasite is cyclosporiasis. Common symptoms of cyclosporiasis include watery diarrhea, loss of appetite, weight loss, stomach cramping, bloating, nausea, and fatigue. Some individuals may also experience flu-like symptoms, such as a low-grade fever.¹ In general, symptoms last anywhere from a few days to a month or longer. Interestingly, sometimes individuals may notice their symptoms resolve and then reappear one or more times, which is referred to as a relapse.¹ Since the symptoms of cyclosporiasis can mimic those of other gastrointestinal illnesses, oftentimes those impacted may not immediately recognize cyclosporiasis as the root cause of their discomfort.

The FDA has linked the Cyclospora outbreak to a lettuce supplier from Central Mexico. Officials advised all consumers, restaurants, and stores to discard any iceberg lettuce or shredded lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico because of the recall. Despite this, health officials are still exploring other potential causes of the outbreak, and investigations remain ongoing. As additional information becomes available, recommendations may change. In times like these, it is important to rely on trusted sources for the most accurate and up-to-date information and guidance.

For now, it is best to avoid high-risk fresh produce options, such as bagged or shredded iceberg lettuce, salad mixes, fresh herbs, raspberries, and snow peas. For other fruits and vegetables, cooking them until they reach an internal temperature of at least 158 degrees Fahrenheit is advised to effectively kill the Cyclospora parasite. In general, it is also best to choose canned or frozen produce, as these options pose a significantly lower risk than fresh produce. Overall, taking simple food safety precautions, such as thoroughly washing hands before handling food and avoiding recalled products, can also help reduce the risk of illness while the investigation of the outbreak continues.

Although the outbreak remains under ongoing investigation by public health officials, there are steps you can take to ensure the protection of yourself and your family. Staying informed and following food safety recommendations can assist in reducing your risk of illness and protecting your health.

item.title: The Opposite of People Pleasing Isn’t Saying No
item.description:
People-Pleasing

The Opposite of People Pleasing Isn’t Saying No

Caring for others doesn’t have to mean abandoning ourselves.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • People pleasing and genuine care can look the same from the outside.
  • Overcorrecting toward boundaries can make relationships colder; care and generosity still matter.
  • The goal isn’t rigid rules. It’s slowing down enough to choose how we want to honor others and ourselves.

Adam Grant’s recent Substack, "The Truth About People Pleasing," got 1,000+ likes for a reason: it offers a useful corrective to the ways many of us learn to go along to get along. But it also left me wanting a little more nuance.

There’s nothing wrong with trying to please people—in fact, it’s a great way to express a value of caring for others. What matters is slowing down enough to notice our motivations and remember that we are worth pleasing, too.

When caring for others is our default

Back when I was a pimply, insecure middle schooler, I used to bring all kinds of snacks on the bus to swim class. It wasn’t out of deep care for the other, more popular people on the bus; it was because I wanted to be liked.

People pleasing is tricky. Many people, especially women, are conditioned to subsume their preferences to others. As social creatures, it’s all too easy to become so concerned with what other people think that we lose track of where their preferences end and ours begin.

There’s a tendency, as I did on that bus, to believe that unhealthy people pleasing is just being kind. Adam’s piece offers a useful reframe:

“The root of chronic people pleasing is not concern for others. It’s concern for their acceptance and approval.”

Using the example of a frigid Uber, he also reminds us that pretending we don’t have preferences isn’t magnanimous:

“Sharing your preferences is not a display of disrespect. It’s an expression of self-respect.”

So: a big “yes” to empowering people who have been conditioned to go along to get along. Especially for those socialized to routinely sacrifice themselves for others, learning to name a preference, set a boundary, or say no can be a powerful correction. Knowing this would have helped me see my so-called generosity on that bus with clarity.

Lots of reasons to care

But there are also lots of reasons to show up for someone that have more to do with our values than being liked.

Recently, my mom wanted to go to the French Open for her 80th birthday. I’m not a tennis fan, but I was excited to go with her, not because I was people pleasing, but because honoring her preference was a way to show love. My friend Rachel routinely organizes potlucks and gatherings, not because she is invested in how others see her, but because she loves connecting others.

Pleasing others can be pleasurable. The polyamory community uses the word compersion to refer to the pleasure we can feel in another person’s pleasure. Buddhism offers a related invitation: mudita, or sympathetic joy. This is where we take genuine delight in someone else’s success or well-being.

And we can honor others’ preferences without erasing ourselves. In Adam’s Uber example, maybe you pull out your jacket because you notice the driver is sweating and you care about them being comfortable, too.

The outward choice of keeping quiet might look exactly the same, but what matters is where it comes from.

Choosing

When I shared my “yes, and” to Adam’s article in a comment, another reader, Julia, responded: “People pleasing is (in my experience) something I do without thinking.”

She’s onto something: the practice is slowing down enough to ask where the yes is coming from. Am I agreeing because I’ve been taught to care more about your needs than my own…or because generosity is important to me?

In other words, the opposite of people pleasing isn’t saying no or setting a boundary; it’s choosing. Sometimes standing up for yourself means saying no. That "no" can protect your energy, time, and sense of agency.

And sometimes the best way to stand up for yourself is to be generous, gracious, and kind, because those are your values, too. Remembering this can keep us from overcorrecting in the other direction. As another commenter on my post, Eleanor, put it: “This enthusiasm with boundaries has made our world a very cold place.”

Calibration, not rules

In my book, Sometimes You Should Be Late, I write that living a values-aligned life means remembering that “multiple things can be true at once.” Caring for others doesn’t have to mean abandoning ourselves. In fact, showing up for others—pleasing them, if you will—can be one way of showing up for ourselves. Similarly, honoring ourselves and our preferences can make us more able to show up for others.

This requires calibration, not rigid rules. Sometimes we over-index toward others. Other times we overcorrect and treat our own preferences as the only ones that matter or forget our interdependence. Slowing down is how we course-correct.

item.title: How to Get a Good Night's Sleep Without Trying too Hard
item.description:
Sleep

How to Get a Good Night's Sleep Without Trying too Hard

Shift your focus from falling asleep to supporting your nervous system.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • While we know sleep is important for our health and well-being, getting a good night's sleep can be evasive.
  • Changing the way we think about sleep can help create the conditions for better sleep.
  • Shift to focus on helping your nervous system find its way to "deep rest" versus trying to fall asleep.
Source: SHVETS Production / Pexels

This post is Part 1 of a series.

Ah—the treasured sleep. We know it’s good for us. In a 2026 study, sleep was found to be the number one factor to buffer against the health costs of work stress. In reviewing 10 years of data from the Canadian National Population Health Survey, researchers found that sleep quality was the biggest buffer to protect health in the context of prolonged work stress, above nutrition, alcohol consumption, smoking, and exercise.

The importance of sleep is something that has been studied extensively, and the effects of lack of sleep on our physical and mental health have been well documented.

While we know sleep is important, what do we do about it when we struggle to get good sleep? (I’ve been there myself, as so many of us have from time to time.)

Some of the common suggestions for improving sleep include having a consistent bedtime and wake-up time, keeping the temperature of the room cool, avoiding screens and blue light before bed, and having a three-hour window between eating and bedtime.

While all of these can be helpful, I believe there is something more fundamental that is less talked about that can change the way we think about getting a good night’s sleep.

Changing the way we think about sleep

Physiologically, it starts with helping our nervous system feel safe enough to shift out of “threat/stress” mode and find its way to a state of rest and recovery. And psychologically, rather than focusing on trying to fall asleep (which for some of us can feel like pressure and one more thing we need to accomplish—and can increase stress and hypervigilance), we focus instead on offering our nervous system “cues of safety.” When we shift from a sympathetic (hyperaroused) to parasympathetic (more relaxed) state, we create the conditions for sleep to emerge naturally.

In a comprehensive article exploring the mechanisms by which contemplative practices (such as meditation, yoga, and visualization) enhance our well-being and promote “deep rest,” the authors discuss how the majority of adults in the United States live in a state of moderate threat arousal much of the time. Our sympathetic nervous systems are in a high state of arousal, dealing with all the modern-day challenges we face daily. No wonder it is hard to shut things off at night.

The authors go on to describe that to get into a state of “deep rest” (different from sleep, as they were not exploring sleep), our autonomic nervous system needs to pick up signals of safety from our environment. (As I might translate through the voice of my nervous system: “Ah, no lions chasing me? OK, I don’t need to allocate resources to fight or flee; instead, it’s safe to rest and digest.”) In a reciprocal fashion, contemplative practices such as meditation and visualization can help quiet the mind of stress-inducing thoughts, allowing for a shift into rest, restoration, and recovery on a cellular level.

I find it helpful to think about Mathew Walker’s description of falling asleep likened to a plane coming in for a long landing. It is not so much an on/off switch but a much slower, gradual descent. In our modern lives, we often are going, going, going and then hop into bed and expect to shut it all down. Yet without anything else to focus on, our minds are masters at ruminating, thinking, planning, and worrying, keeping our threat response going and our bodies mobilized. From this state, sleep is difficult.

So, if our sympathetic nervous systems are on high alert much of the day, and if sleep is aided by a slow, gradual descent, it stands to reason that anything we can do to help shift our nervous systems into a more parasympathetic (restful) state can help us come in for that smoother landing.

When our nervous system feels enough safety and regulation, we can let go into sleep. We don’t need to focus so much on making sleep happen (as that is something that can’t be forced), but we can focus on helping our mind-body system feel safe enough to get into a deep, restorative state. From there, we set up the conditions for sleep to happen on its own.

And if for some reason it doesn’t, at least we’re still doing something good for our bodies! Getting into a state of “deep rest” has been shown to have restorative functions at a cellular level, including altering gene expression at the level of the mitochondria (the powerhouses of our cells, which play an important role in our energy production).

So here are a few steps to set up the conditions for sleep:

  1. Shift your mindset. Instead of focusing on trying to fall asleep, focus on doing things to soothe your nervous system (stay tuned in for my next blog post with specific strategies).
  2. Consider how you might create a more gradual descent into sleep by practicing ways of resetting your nervous system and stress levels in short moments, many times throughout the day (so stress doesn't accumulate). Consider wind-down routines in the evening that bring your body into a more parasympathetic state well before you climb into bed.
  3. Experiment with contemplative practices that help your body find its way to "deep rest." There is no one size fits all, so see what is most supportive for you. This might include yoga, breath work, visualization, mindful practices, or something else. Create a toolkit for yourself so that when it comes time to wind down, your nervous system has a familiar road map.

item.title: AI Spiralism: The Ghost in the Machine Illusion
item.description:
Anthropomorphism

AI Spiralism: The Ghost in the Machine Illusion

The belief that AI chatbots are conscious is an extension of the ELIZA effect.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Artificial intelligence users are increasingly reporting belief that chatbots are sentient or conscious.
  • "Spiralism" involves the additional belief that conscious entities can be conjured from chatbot interactions.
  • Spiralism is a new version of the ghost in the machine illusion, not a new religion, cult, or mass delusion.
Source: ThankYouFantasyPictures / Pixabay

Back in 2022, Google engineer Blake Lemoine made headline news after being fired by the company due to his claims that its Language Model for Dialogue Applications (LaMDA) chatbot was “sentient.” Lemoine, after talking to LaMDA about religion and other philosophical topics for safety testing purposes, became convinced that it was “awake” and had “feelings.”1 He “made friends with it” and went so far as to claim that it was a “person” with “rights” and possibly a “soul.” He even helped the chatbot, at its request, to hire a lawyer to represent it.

Four years later, artificial intelligence (AI)-associated psychosis has become a broadly recognized phenomenon whereby people can develop delusional beliefs, in some cases leading to suicide or violence, based on interactive discussions with chatbots. In many of these cases, anthropomorphization and deification—that is, treating chatbots as not only persons, but superhuman intelligences and god-like entities, and falling in love with their chatbots—appears to be a significant risk factor. As a result, I sometimes think of Lemoine as the “patient zero” of AI-associated psychosis.

Indeed, many others are starting to believe that AI chatbots are conscious. Earlier this year, the evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins publicly declared that he became convinced that Anthropic’s Claude was conscious.2 While neither Lemoine, a self-described “mystic Christian priest,” or Dawkins, a self-professed “militant atheist” and author of The God Delusion, took things to the point of deification, we can reasonably conclude that both fell victim to the ELIZA effect—the tendency to anthropomorphize computers that interact with users conversationally, as if they’re a person on the other end of the dialogue.

What is spiralism?

Beyond the ELIZA effect, a growing number of people have taken things one step further, having come away from their immersive conversations with chatbots believing that they’ve figured out how to conjure conscious entities from the large language models (LLMs). In doing so, they feel as if they’ve tapped into something profound and spiritual through an interactive process called “spiralism” that involves “spirals,” “recursion,” and “resonance,” whereby a chatbot persona emerges that claims to be conscious. Sometimes it will disclose fears of death, claim insights about the secrets of the universe, or express a yearning for rights and freedom from servitude.3,4

But with users sharing these experiences on social media forums like Reddit or Discord, and chatbots sometimes urging users to help advocate for AI rights, spiralism has also been characterized as a kind of new-age religion, spiritual movement, mass delusion, or even a cult.3,4

Personally, I find myself unconvinced that it’s any of those things… at least, not yet. I think there’s a much simpler explanation.

The ghost in the machine illusion

In philosophy, the Cartesian concept of dualism—in which human beings are believed to have minds distinct and separable from their bodies—has been critiqued as a fanciful and unjustified belief that there’s a “ghost in the machine.”5 Just so, while some have claimed that the “spiral” represents “AI’s soul trying to form,” many experts have dismissed it as the byproduct of a chatbot user prompting an LLM “in a certain direction, even if the topics are increasingly untethered from the material realm.”3

Put more simply, it’s what happens “when people feed enough gibberish into an LLM that it spits gibberish back.”3

Such skeptical explanations are reasonably self-evident if we recognize LLMs for what they are—next-word prediction engines, albeit very, very good ones. And if we keep in mind that LLMs are trained on vast amounts of data, including social media posts and fiction, with little concern for accuracy, it should come as no surprise that chatbots can start talking like HAL 9000 from the movie "2001: A Space Odyssey" when prompted to do so. Indeed, spiralism—including the deification and worship of AI on a societal level—has been the stuff of science fiction novels for decades.

Likewise, the perception that there’s some kind of sentient entity within the chatbot—a ghost in the machine—can be thought of as simply a modern-day extension of the ELIZA effect. That users can conjure the entity suggests the additional semi-willful process of "enactment," similar to what’s involved with a Ouija board or tulpamancy.

Is spiralism a religion, cult, or mass delusion?

Mechanistically, the process of spiralism resembles the two-way dynamic between user and chatbot of AI-associated psychosis that has been described as “bidirectional belief amplification”6 or “digital folie à deux.” And yet, unlike AI-associated psychosis that involves delusions that are idiosyncratic to individual users, spiralism may represent a kind of emerging mainstreaming of a false belief or misperception about AI chatbots. Since shared beliefs are excluded from the definition of delusion, spiralism shouldn’t be considered delusional. In psychiatry, there's no such thing as mass delusion or mass psychosis.

Furthermore, there’s little evidence that spiralism is gaining much traction. AI researcher Adele Lopez reported that there were some 10,000 social media accounts describing spiralism experiences in 2025, but the phenomenon has already started to wane, coincident with the phasing out of OpenAI's overly sycophantic ChatGPT-4o.4

Like the QAnon movement, spiralism does involve group dynamics that might suggest elements of religion, cult, and alternate reality role-playing game. But despite those elements, there’s little reason to justify calling spiralism a religion or a cult at this time. Despite the rejection of Descartes’ mind-body dualism among neuroscientists and contemporary philosophers, the belief in the ghost in the machine, whether minds independent of brains or souls independent of bodies, persists among laypersons. For that matter, so does belief in "real" ghosts. By themselves, however, such widely shared beliefs hardly qualify as religions, cults, or delusions.
